Modern-Day Propaganda in the Age of AI May Be Propaganda That Never Asks Everyone to Believe the Same Thing Here's some interesting food for thought to consider regarding propaganda in the digital age. Take the data center problem, as an example. One person might see jobs, tax revenue, and technological progress. Another could see massive buildings consuming electricity and water while giving little back to the surrounding community. Someone else could see national security: if we want to compete in AI, we need the infrastructure to run it. And then there are people worried about mass surveillance. They understand exactly what these systems could make possible, more data collection, more behavioral tracking, more power concentrated in private and government hands. But even they could acquiesce or support the data centers in the near future. Why? Because they might be influenced to believe that the technology will come either way. Better to build it here, where it can be regulated. Better to stay ahead of foreign competitors. Better to support the infrastructure now and fight over how it’s used later. And as construction expands, it could embolden small radical groups to take violent or illegal action against the centers. If that begins trending, the group would become the story. Anyone raising concerns about surveillance, water, energy, or corporate power could be pressured to distance themselves from the opposition. Nobody wants to be associated with extremists or labeled anti-progress. So the surveillance skeptic will go silent to avoid social scrutiny and vote rationally to choose the lesser of evils. The nationalists will vote for technological independence. The anxious voters will choose security. The optimist will choose progress. Different beliefs. Different emotional triggers. The same outcome: the data centers expand. That’s what makes modern propaganda so unsettling when it becomes possible to map and understand clustered behaviors. A population doesn’t have to share one belief to produce one future. It can be divided into different emotional camps, fear, pride, anger, hope, while still being guided toward the same decision by taking advantage of media feeds and our digital behaviors. So control may not be in the message these days. A lot of it could exist in the destination, itself.

AI lab offers free plumbing and HVAC repairs across three cities to train AI robots Robotics An AI company called HUMXN is trying something interesting: it's offering free plumbing, electrical, HVAC, and other home services to qualifying homeowners in exchange for collecting real-world training data. The program is launching in Minneapolis, Chicago, and Miami. During the jobs, technicians use wearable recording technology to capture how they inspect problems, choose tools, and complete repairs. The goal is to help AI systems learn how skilled workers interact with the physical world, rather than relying entirely on text and images from the internet. This makes sense when you think about it. A robot can't learn to fix a complicated plumbing issue just by reading about plumbing. It needs data about the actual steps, decisions, tools, and unexpected situations involved. I'm curious about one thing, though: Could collecting real-world work data like this be the missing piece in making physical AI and robots genuinely useful in everyday life? And would you let a technician record their work inside your home in exchange for a free repair?

We've spent years teaching people not to trust input. Now we're giving AI agents access to our entire workspace. A coding agent might read a repository, inspect environment variables, execute shell commands, install dependencies, and access external services, all this in one workflow sometimes. The interesting security question isn't just whether the model can be manipulated. It's what damage a compromised or confused agent is actually allowed to do. If you were designing an agent sandbox from scratch, what permission would you refuse to grant by default?

GitHub makes Agentic Autofix generally available for code scanning alerts GitHub's Agentic Autofix is now generally available for GitHub Code Security and GitHub Advanced Security customers on Enterprise Cloud. When a user assigns a code-scanning alert to Copilot, it explores relevant files, proposes a fix, reruns CodeQL, and opens a draft pull request for review. The useful limit is that this is still a review workflow, not an automatic merge. Enterprise admins must enable the policy, and usage consumes AI Credits from the Code Security budget plus GitHub Actions minutes. It supports alerts on the repository default branch, not alerts found only on pull requests or other branches. The practical question is less whether an agent can write a patch and more how teams budget, review, and measure fixes before they merge. Sources: GitHub Changelog: https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-15-agentic-autofix-for-code-scanning-alerts-general-availability/ GitHub Community: https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/209845

The AI personas that will work are the ones that admit they’re fake Noticed everyone building AI influencers and characters try to pass as real is playing it backwards. The ones that build a real audience long-term will be openly artificial. The audience knows it's a character, the character performs like it's real, and everybody's in on it. Pro wrestling figured this out decades ago — old kayfabe meant pretending it was real. Modern kayfabe is the crowd knowing and playing along anyway, and the attachment got stronger, not weaker. Meanwhile the "totally a real person" AI accounts all die the same way: one slip, one uncanny detail, and it turns into a scandal instead of a story. Am I wrong? Is the honesty actually the product — or do people only care when there's a chance they're being fooled?
